summary: This ExxonMobil report, dated Jan. 8, 2024, digests global energy demand through three drivers (technology, policy, consumer preferences) and then projects demand to 2050 by sector, fuel and transportation mode. It draws on ExxonMobil's Global Outlook charts and compares its outlook with IEA and IPCC scenarios. Most of the growth is attributed to developing countries, while efficiency gains and electrification offset demand in developed economies.
one_line: ExxonMobil report on the three drivers of energy demand and its 2050 projections by sector, fuel and transportation.
key_facts: Global energy demand reaches about 660 quadrillion Btu in 2050, up about 15% versus 2021, reflecting a growing population and rising prosperity.
Residential and commercial primary energy demand declines by approximately 15% to 2050 as efficiency improvements offset the energy needs of a growing population.
Developing countries account for more than 100% of the global energy demand growth.
The combined share of energy used in the U.S. and Europe declines from about 30% in 2021 to about 20% in 2050.
Renewables and nuclear contribute around 70% of incremental energy supplies to meet demand growth.
Natural gas grows over the period, reaching almost 30% of all demand.
Coal use drops below 15% global share as China and developed nations shift toward lower-emission sources.
Global transportation-related energy demand is expected to grow by more than 30% from 2021 to 2050.
Aviation demand sees the highest compounded annual growth rate at about 3.5% from 2021 to 2050.
In 2021, the global light-duty fleet was about 1.2 billion vehicles, with 16 million (1.3%) being plug-in hybrids, battery electric, or fuel cell.
By 2050, advanced vehicles grow to approximately 44% of the fleet (920 million) and more than 50% of new car sales.
In the Outlook, battery-electric vehicles are projected to be 24% of all new car sales by 2035 and 36% by 2050.
A sensitivity assuming 100% battery electric vehicle sales from 2035 onward would reduce global oil demand (excluding biofuels) to around 2010 levels.
If fuel efficiency improved at historical rates, fuel demand in 2050 may be almost 3 million barrels per day higher.
Asia Pacific leads commercial transportation growth, accounting for more than 40% of commercial transportation energy demand by 2050.
